newsitem.title: UK: ERM tension builds as stg drags punt to the roof.
newsitem.headline: ERM tension builds as stg drags punt to the roof.

text.p: The volatility of the British pound is once again creating problems for the European Union's exchange rate mechanism (ERM)-- even though the UK remains resolutely outside the multilateral currency system.
Sterling's magnetic pull on the Irish punt is causing tensions not seen since the crises of 1992/1993, when the pound itself was forced out of the grid and the system was revamped.

This year, a sterling-driven appreciation of the punt to the limits of its permitted ERM fluctuation bands has raised speculation that the newly-elected Irish government may seek a revaluation of the punt's central target rate.
This would be seen in many quarters as an effective reversal of the punt's 10 percent devaluation in January 1993, forced by sterling's collapse the previous September.

The similar business cycles in the UK and Ireland and strong trade links between the two countries have seen Irish interest rates stay among the highest in Europe and the punt follow sterling's surge in an attempt to balance terms of trade.

"There is a very compelling argument for a punt revaluation in the ERM from the point of view of a tightening of monetary policy and inflation risk associated with its fall against sterling," said Joe Prendergast, head of global currency strategy at CSFB.
There is still a firm belief among the Irish authorities that the devaluation of 1993 was unjustified, he said.
Traders said there was speculation on Friday the Bank of France sold punts for French francs to keep both currencies within their permitted fluctuation bands.
The French franc currently occupies the foot of the ERM grid and is trading about 13 percent weaker than its central rate against the punt, just shy of the 15 percent limits.

The punt traded over 2.70 marks on Friday for the first time since 1993 as sterling vaulted over 3.0 marks. The punt retained the bulk of that move on Monday and is now about 12 percent above its 2.4111 ERM central rate.

But while the punt has soared against continental European currencies, it has weakened sharply against sterling - providing the booming economy with an anomalous fillip from a more favourable terms of trade with its major single trading partner.

This potentially inflationary impact, unless stymied by a broad-based revaluation of the punt, could cause problems for Ireland's chances of meeting the entry criteria for European monetary union if it fuels a divergence in inflationary trends from the rest of Europe, analysts said.

For these same reasons, the authorities in Dublin are prevented from cutting interest rates to cap the punt within the ERM and this will leave the onus of exchange rate management on intervention, they said.
Yet, likely or not, analysts agree a punt revaluation would be littered with problems.
"We believe the case for a punt revaluation is not strong enough. A change of ERM parities this close to EMU would risk opening a whole can of worms," said Martin Brookes, economist at Goldman Sachs.

Brookes said he believes the authorities will opt to live with the status quo for now and official confirmation later this year that ERM midrates will be used as EMU conversion rates is likely to see the punt ease back towards its existing parity.
First, a change of the punt's ERM pegging may also be seen to prejudice Ireland's participation in the monetary union from the start date in 1999.

With just 18 months to go to EMU day, the Maastricht Treaty requirement of two years of exchange rate stability within the ERM may be breached by a revaluation unless the words "without devaluing" were read to the letter, analysts said.

Even if Ireland were allowed to start EMU on time at a higher rate, there are domestic concerns about institutionalising a stronger ERM parity because these rates will most likely be used as the eventual EMU conversion rates.
Fixing at a higher rate into EMU would not then allow a cyclical readjustment of the punt when the booming local economy slows or when sterling reverses.
An upward revaluation of the punt, meantime, would also involve the first ever devaluation of a bilateral German mark exchange rate peg in the ERM's 18-year history.
This could prove to be a symbolically difficult move for German authorities trying to sooth public angst about the loss of the mark in the run-up to EMU, some analysts argue.
The new Irish finance minister Charlie McCreevy has refused to be drawn on the issue.

The next setting of the automatically determined "Green" currency rates - the rates used for the EU's system of agricultural subsidies - is on August 20 and another revaluation fo the Green punt rate would put the spot rate's ERM position back in focus domestically.
